sn44.1:1.1: The “undeclared points” are a stock series of propositions typically raised by non-Buddhists. It seems they formed a kind of scheme for evaluating and positioning different philosophies, which were assumed to answer them definitively. They are discussed many times in the Suttas, eg. [sn16.12](), [sn24.15]()–18, [sn33.1]()–55.
sn44.1:1.2: Khemā was extolled as the foremost nun in great wisdom ([an1.236]()); her verses are at [thig6.3](); see [sn17.24:1.7](). | Toraṇavatthu (“the site of the arch”) appears only here.
sn44.1:1.5: Pasenadi uses the default masculine forms, the significance of which becomes apparent below.
sn44.1:3.5: Pasenadi was used to having philosophical conversations with his wife, Queen Mallikā ([sn3.8:1.2]()).
sn44.1:4.1: The king bows to the nun, just as he would to the Buddha.
sn44.1:4.2: An awakened one, whether the Buddha or anyone else, exists after death, for example in heaven or an eternal state of Nirvana. | Here “realized one” (_tathāgata_) pertains to any arahant, as at [sn54.12](). The Pali commentary says that a “living being” (_satta_) is meant. However, _tathāgata_ and _satta_ are exact verbal parallels: _tathā_ (“real”) + _gata_ (“come to the state of”) and _sa_ (“real”) + _tta_ (“state of”). Thus it seems likely that this was originally intended as a mere verbal gloss to resolve the compound. That it does not mean just any sentient being is established at [sn22.86:1.5]().
sn44.1:4.5: A sage ceases to exist at the time of death. This assumes there is an enduring “self” that is done away with.
sn44.1:4.8: This kind of “both A and not A” statements are not meant to be paradoxical or mystical. Rather, they represent some state that combines elements of both. For example, their body does not exist but their mind does.
sn44.1:4.11: Likewise, “neither A nor not A” is not meant to be a paradox, but to indicate something that cannot be characterized by the original term. For example, a sage persists after death in a subtle state that is not what we normally consider existence.
sn44.1:6.3: Accountant (_gaṇaka_), finger-tallier (_muddika_), and reckoner (_saṅkhāyako_) are terms for the job that used to be called “computer”.
sn44.1:13.2: Compare AN 11.7 for variant viggayhissati. Also, note that the idiom “yatra hi nama”, like other idiomatic uses of “nama”, often has an emphatic or exclamatory force.
